A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same electron-density-based SCF acceleration method and SCFbench study. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison despite the title change and expanded experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original SCFbench experiments, functional and basis-set transfer tests, auxiliary-basis analysis, and WALoss experiments in Section 6 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds larger-molecule evaluations, normalization experiments, runtime measurements, direct-to-solution accuracy results, and QHFlow experiments.

M1.justification: The auxiliary-density representation, modified NequIP/QHNet prediction heads, MAE-plus-RMSE training loss, and density-to-Fock construction remain unchanged. The hybrid/meta-GGA approximations already appeared in v1 Appendix C. Normalization and direct-to-solution evaluations do not establish changes to the proposed initializer.

E1.justification: v3 Section 6.2 extends evaluation beyond SCFbench's molecules of up to 60 atoms to 110 QMugs molecules containing 100–200 atoms, a 703-atom Glycine-100 polypeptide, and a 905-atom polypropylene chain. This substantially broadens molecular-size coverage and introduces polymer/polypeptide scenarios.

E2.justification: QHFlow, previously only discussed as related work, is trained and evaluated on SCFbench in v3 Appendix K/Table 10. Existing QHNet Hamiltonian, density-matrix, and WALoss comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the stated ID evaluation subset from 1,000 molecules to 1% of the test set, although retained result tables have identical values; the PDFs do not establish whether experiments were rerun. Added protocols include end-to-end GPU timing, single-diagonalization energy/orbital-error evaluation, and the larger-system tests, whose Table 2 explicitly averages RIC over converged molecules only.

E4.justification: v3 adds a density-normalization ablation, initialization-cost decomposition, direct-to-solution error analysis, and two large-system case studies. Appendix B reports OOD RIC changing from 66.68% to 67.81% with normalization. The original D-Glucose auxiliary-basis analysis and WALoss sweep remain, under new appendix/table numbers.

E5.justification: No new repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are reported. Figure 1's shaded bands are retained, and the added timing and accuracy results introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained tables preserve their numerical entries, but substantial new results appear. Table 2 reports 73.42–81.77% RIC with 100% convergence on QMugs; the 703/905-atom cases require 10/8 iterations versus minao's 17/12. Figure 4 reports approximately 1.3× end-to-end speedup, Table 9 reports NequIP-L OOD energy MAE of 7.5e-4 Hartree, and Table 10 reports QHFlow ID/OOD RICs of 56.80%/146.97%.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(17), including density-projection and Fock-construction derivations, are retained. The added normalization and SCF-consistency discussions explain standard physical requirements and existing operations without introducing a new proof or substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the demonstrated transferability claim from molecules of up to 60 atoms to approximately 900-atom polymers and polypeptides without retraining. The central method and dataset contributions remain. Although the title drops 'Universally', the abstract retains the aspiration of a universally transferable accelerator.

C2.justification: New appendices explain retaining SCF for orbital-based observables, restoration of electron number through orbital occupation, and the initialization bottleneck from XC grid evaluation. They distinguish chemical-accuracy energy predictions from precise SCF convergence. Appendix L also qualifies the largest-system evidence: the tested chains contain repetitive units, leaving chemically diverse large systems unverified.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the coming-soon project notice with a SCFbench dataset link and reports release. It additionally specifies DIIS space size 8, no level shifting or damping, the V100/GPU4PySCF timing setup, Python integration implementation, and use of QHFlow's QH9 defaults. Existing architecture and training hyperparameter tables are unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for QMugs, another electron-density prediction study, GPU4PySCF, and efficient equivariant computations. Section 3.2 revises attribution of kernel-based versus equivariant density-matrix methods. Appendix K positions QHFlow as potentially complementary while retaining the paper's central transferability argument.

P1.justification: The title and parts of the abstract/introduction are revised, related-work attribution is clarified, and explanatory subsections are added. A large-system subsection and additional appendices extend the structure, but most existing prose, the main section sequence, and the conclusion remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the displayed evidence with a QMugs scalability table, a two-panel runtime and initialization-breakdown figure, and direct-to-solution and QHFlow tables. Figure 2 changes from a small text-wrapped inset to a large full-width display. Retained tables are relocated or renumbered, and the extended-results caption clarifies metric units.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the paper's central scalability and practical-acceleration claims: v1 stopped at 60 atoms and iteration ratios, whereas v3 adds larger-system tests and end-to-end timing that includes initialization overhead. The normalization analysis, QHFlow comparison, and explicit limitations further improve evaluation and interpretation. The unexplained ID sample change despite identical retained tables remains a reproducibility concern, but the new evidence addresses important gaps and provides a substantial net improvement.
